subject: site abundance from predict() when assuming a zero inflated Poisson error structure and model pcount (N-Mixture)

messages.author: c52d6613363308cd
messages.subject: site abundance from predict() when assuming a zero inflated Poisson error structure and model pcount (N-Mixture)
parts:
I have recently had a brief email exchange with Andy Royle about some
modeling I am doing using N-mixture models. The question came up as
to whether the predict() function in umarked returned the mean
abundance in occupied sites (lambda) or the mean abundance weighted by
the occupancy rate (lambda*probability of site occupancy). Andy
couldn't recall and suggested I write a simple model to see. After I
did the work Andy suggested I post the results here for others to
see. Hopefully it will benefit someone.


Hi Andy. I did the simulation you suggested (code below). I thought
you would like to know that It looks like predict() gives the lambda
unweighted by psi. I also see that the interpretation of the psi
parameter in unmarked is a little tricky (see bottom of code).

Thanks again!

Lew



sites=1000
reps=20
int=2
slope=.025
truepsi=0.25
truedet=.3

x=(runif(sites,27,32))
state=rpois(sites,exp(int+slope*x))*rbinom(sites,1,truepsi)

obs=matrix(NA,sites,reps)
for(j in 1:reps){
for(i in 1:sites){
obs[i,j]=rbinom(1,state[i],truedet)
}
}
#obs

SCovs=data.frame(bottom=x)

counts=obs
n.mix.dat=unmarkedFramePCount(y=counts,siteCovs=SCovs)
mod=pcount(~1 ~bottom,data=n.mix.dat,K=25,mixture=c("ZIP"),engine="C")

backTransform(mod,'det')
coef(mod)

x2=seq(27,32,length.out=20)
eststate=predict(mod,'state',data.frame(bottom=x2))

plot(x,state)
lines(x2,eststate[,1])
lines(x2,exp(int+slope*seq(27,32,length.out=20)),col='blue')

#true psi is:
truepsi

#this is expit of estimated psi:
1/(1+exp(-coef(mod)[4]))

#this is 1- expit of estimated psi (complement):
1-1/(1+exp(-coef(mod)[4]))

#THIS MUST BE WHY IT IS CALLED "Zero Inflation" in the model
summary..... BUT NAMING THE PARAMETER "psi" IS CONFUSING

messages.subject: Re: site abundance from predict() when assuming a zero inflated Poisson error structure and model pcount (N-Mixture)
parts:
I’ve also been doing some simulations with pcount and zip, based on the simulation presented with the pcount function in the unmarked 0.9-7 manual manual (p. 48).  Unlike the predict function, it appears that the empirical Bayes function ‘ranef’ gives estimates that are the mean (or mode) abundance weighted by occupancy for zip models.  I’ve noticed that when p(detection) is reasonably high (say 0.5, as in scenario 1 of my script), pcount with zip does a good job of modeling the zip data.  When p(detection) is low (say 0.1, as in scenario 2 of my script), it doesn’t necessarily do so well.  This is understandable because when p(detection) is low, it must be difficult to differentiate between unoccupied sites and occupied sites that happened never to produce a detection.  The latter situation seems to apply to a real data set that I’m dealing with on clapper rails.  I’m inclined to go with the basic Poisson model for the rails rather than the zip (even though the zip is superior by the usual model comparison criteria) because the basic Poisson seems at worst to give somewhat of an underestimate of overall abundance, whereas the zip potentially gives a large overestimate when p(detection) is low.  I suppose that I could also do an occupancy model in conjunction with the basic Poisson model to get a handle on site occupancy rate.

 

My simulation script is below. Any comments (including on my thoughts on using the basic Poisson for the rails) or corrections are welcome.  BTW using ‘mean(bup(ranef …’ in the script may be arguable when the bups aren’t normally distributed but median or mode didn’t seem to work obviously better.   

 

RK

 

library(unmarked)

# Simulate data

# scenario 1:  true detection p = 0.5

# scenario 2: true detection p = 0.1

set.seed(27) #This seed produces data that exemplify the issue with low p(detect);

                      #results with other seeds may differ.

nSites <- 1000

nVisits <- 3

lambda <- 3

psi <- 0.33

# p <- 0.50    #scenario 1 good result

  p <- 0.10    #scenario 2 not so good result

N <- rpois(nSites, lambda) # latent abundance

y <- matrix(NA, nSites, nVisits)

for(j in 1:nVisits) y[,j] <- rbinom(nSites, N, p)

for(i in 1:nSites) if(runif(1,0,1)<psi) y[i,1:3] <- 0

 

umf <- unmarkedFramePCount(y=y)

summary(umf)

 

# Fit a ZIP model

fmZIP <- pcount(~1 ~1, umf, mixture="ZIP", K=100)

summary(fmZIP)

(plogis(coef(fmZIP, type="det")))# Should be close to p

(plogis(confint(fmZIP,type="det")))

(plogis(coef(fmZIP, type="psi"))) # Should be close to psi

(plogis(confint(fmZIP, type="psi")))

(exp(coef(fmZIP,type="state")))  # Should be close to lambda

(exp(confint(fmZIP,type="state")))

#2 ways to estimate overall mean abundance:

(exp(coef(fmZIP,type="state")))*(1-(plogis(coef(fmZIP, type="psi"))))

(mean(bup(ranef(fmZIP))))

colMeans(confint(ranef(fmZIP)))

hist(bup(ranef(fmZIP)))

 

# Fit a basic Poisson model

fmPois <- pcount(~1 ~1, umf, mixture="P", K=100)

summary(fmPois)

(plogis(coef(fmPois, type="det")))

(plogis(confint(fmPois,type="det"))) #

(exp(coef(fmPois,type="state")))

(exp(confint(fmPois,type="state")))

mean(bup(ranef(fmPois)))

colMeans(confint(ranef(fmPois)))
